title: Reading Guide: .NET E-Commerce Monolith
overview: This monolith demonstrates a classic modular monolith with clear bounded contexts but tight coupling through a shared database. Understanding the code requires following the data flow from controllers through services to the god DbContext.

guidedTour.title: Start Here: The Entry Point
guidedTour.description: ASP.NET Core minimal hosting setup. Registers services, configures the DbContext with an in-memory database, and sets up the HTTP pipeline. This is where all dependencies are wired together.
guidedTour.next: Look at Data/ShopDbContext.cs to see what this DbContext owns

guidedTour.title: The God Context Problem
guidedTour.description: This single DbContext owns ALL entities across ALL domains - Products, Categories, Customers, StockItems, Payments, Orders. This is the primary coupling point preventing independent deployment of services.
guidedTour.next: See Orders/OrderService.cs for how this coupling enables (and requires) the problematic transaction

guidedTour.title: The CreateOrder Saga
guidedTour.description: This is the core business workflow that MUST work differently in microservices. Currently it spans 4 domains in one ACID transaction. In the decomposed version, this becomes a distributed saga with compensation.
keyLines: await _db.SaveChanges() - ONE commit for ALL changes
guidedTour.migrationNote: In microservices: each service has its own database, so this workflow becomes CreateOrderSaga with outbox pattern and compensation handlers.
guidedTour.next: Check Inventory/InventoryService.cs for a concurrency bug

guidedTour.title: Race Condition in Inventory
guidedTour.description: The Reserve() method has a classic read-check-then-write race condition. Two concurrent orders for the last item in stock can BOTH succeed (oversell). This bug should be fixed during decomposition.
guidedTour.fix: Add RowVersion for optimistic concurrency, or use raw SQL with WHERE quantity >= @quantity
guidedTour.next: See Payments/PaymentService.cs for another quality issue

guidedTour.title: String Enums Anti-Pattern
guidedTour.description: The Payment.Status property is a bare string instead of an enum. This allows typos ('Sucess' vs 'Success') and prevents compile-time validation.
guidedTour.antipattern: public string Status { get; set; } // Should be PaymentStatus enum
guidedTour.fix: Create PaymentStatus enum { Pending, Completed, Failed, Refunded }
guidedTour.next: Examine Catalog/CatalogService.cs to see a well-isolated service

guidedTour.title: Clean Bounded Context: Catalog
guidedTour.description: The catalog service is a good example of a cleanly bounded context. It only touches Product and Category entities, has no outbound dependencies, and can be extracted with minimal changes.
guidedTour.next: See the Catalog controller for the API surface

guidedTour.title: API Layer: Catalog Controller
guidedTour.description: Simple REST controller exposing the catalog. In microservices, this becomes the catalog-service's own HTTP interface, called by other services via HTTP client instead of direct method calls.
guidedTour.migrationNote: In target: OrderService will call this via typed HTTP client instead of injecting CatalogService

guidedTour.title: Summary: What Makes This Hard
guidedTour.description:
The decomposition challenge isn't the code complexity - each service is simple. The challenge is:

1. God DbContext couples everything
2. PlaceOrder is one ACID transaction across 4 domains
3. Other services' direct method calls become HTTP calls
4. Data consistency becomes eventual, not immediate
5. Testing requires running multiple services
guidedTour.benefits: Independent deployment, technology choice, scaling, team ownership
guidedTour.tradeoffs: Operational complexity, eventual consistency, distributed tracing needed

architecturalDecisions.rationale: This is a demo fixture. Real apps would use SQL Server / PostgreSQL.
Keeping the monolith simple to focus on decomposition mechanics. The target microservices will add repositories.
architecturalDecisions.impact: Services directly use DbContext - this coupling is intentional for the demo

architecturalDecisions.rationale: OrderService.PlaceOrder is INTENTIONALLY complex to demonstrate saga decomposition. This is the teaching moment.
